doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Stranded in Salt Lake City with Jimmy Mundy's band
summary: Mundy's new band with the 4 Step Brothers ran out of money in Salt Lake City, seven stayed, found a gig at a black club, and Hamilton wired his sister for bus fare home.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Now we’re really getting into the -- we’re going to stop. So, you know, during the break I just wanted to, or now that we’re off break I wanted to come back and fill in a few more of the chronological gaps. One of the biographies mentions when you got out of the military, that you actually joined Jimmy Mundy and then got stranded in Salt Lake City.
That’s right.
So is that a story you want to fill in some gaps first? It says here it was 1946.
Okay. After playing with -- who did I say I did the show with? Floyd Ray’s band -- it was Jimmy Mundy?
Uh-huh.

Jimmy Mundy organized a band and I got a call from him and he wanted me ­ - and I joined his band and the show was the 4 Step Brothers. They were the headliners and singers, and, you know, the whole package, and our first gig was in Salt Lake City.
First gig.
The first gig with the band. And the money ran out so we got stranded there, man.
In Salt Lake City.
Salt Lake City, and if you’ve ever been black in Salt Lake City -­
You won’t go back.
Especially during the ’40s, ‘46s -- what was that in, ‘46?
In ‘46, man -­
It could be 2006. I don’t think it’s going to make any difference.
Man, let me tell you, at that time man, those people -- their religion said the reason we were black is because we sinned. That was God’s curse on us.
The mark of Cain.

Yeah. So anyway we went -- there was seven of us. Everybody left, but there was seven of us left, me, Hawk, the tenor player, the piano player. In other words we had a group, and we laid around there for three or four days and somebody came up with a gig. There was a place outside of Salt Lake, outside of whatever it was, but it had to be -- it was a black club strangely enough but it wasn’t in the town, I mean, you know, in the city, and the guy hired us to play there. And I went two days without eating man, and I found a nickel.
The money ran out so you didn’t have any money.
I didn’t have any -- none of us had any money.
None of you had money.

None of us had any money, man. And I found a nickel -- this is the truth man, I found a nickel on the ground and I bought an ice cream sandwich. So we made this gig man, and this dude -- Hawk the piano player asked to do -- you know, after gig was over he said man, we want our booze, right. This dude said your booze? Hawk said yeah. So he pulls out his gun, he pulls out his Roscoe man. He pulls out his gun and he says, I’m going to (unintelligible) you. So man, finally I called my sister and she sent me some money, train fare -- bus fare rather, and here it is me and all these drums. You know, I had cases -- I made my way back to LA. That was an experience.
Okay, so that’s why that’s in there. And now we know the rest of the story.
Yeah.
